what_changed.headline: Energy shock is tightening global financial conditions
what_changed.significance: Middle East escalation has pushed oil, refined-product and European gas prices sharply higher; global long-end yields have also risen.
what_changed.transmission: Higher energy costs raise inflation risks and rate expectations, while tighter financial conditions pressure duration-sensitive assets.

what_changed.headline: Canada held policy at 2.25% amid competing growth and inflation risks
what_changed.significance: Q2 GDP rose 3.3% and July unemployment was 6.4%, but excess supply remains and US tariffs increase uncertainty.
what_changed.transmission: Resilient activity and higher energy inflation keep tightening risks alive, while tariffs argue against an immediate hawkish shift.

executive_decisions.development: Treat the energy shock as the primary cross-asset driver.
executive_decisions.why_it_matters: Oil and refined-product disruption can extend inflation pressure and delay monetary easing.
executive_decisions.transmission: Higher yields and input costs challenge long-duration equities and bonds; energy assets benefit from scarcity.

executive_decisions.development: Reassess duration exposure, especially at the long end.
executive_decisions.why_it_matters: Fiscal supply, higher real yields and energy inflation are jointly pressuring long maturities.
executive_decisions.transmission: Long-end underperformance can tighten financial conditions and weigh on rate-sensitive equities.

macro_themes.market_implication: Favors energy and selected commodity exposure but pressures duration, rate-sensitive equities and non-yielding assets.

themes.title: Supply-driven inflation versus restrictive policy
themes.implication: The combination can keep rates higher for longer while weakening real household income and cyclical demand.

themes.title: Global yield and fiscal-risk repricing
themes.implication: The shock is negative for duration and broad risk appetite, but its FX effect is ambiguous where higher yields are interpreted as fiscal rather than monetary strength.

themes.title: AI adoption is broadening, but near-term labour displacement remains limited
themes.implication: The evidence supports gradual labour transformation rather than an immediate employment shock, while investment exposure is more credible through infrastructure and productivity channels than through an assumed aggregate-demand boom.

themes.title: AI investment is becoming a cross-market financing and duration shock
themes.implication: Favourable AI demand does not eliminate financing risk: supply, concentration, leverage and delayed revenue realization can raise credit premia and pressure long-duration assets.

themes.title: Scarcity has broadened the commodity inflation channel
themes.implication: Commodity exposure may diversify inflation risk, but individual markets remain vulnerable to supply normalisation, weather improvement or weaker growth.
